n: Solomon made a huge bronze altar for burnt offerings, about 30 feet square and 15 feet high — far larger than the tabernacle altar. It stood in the courtyard where the people brought their sacrifices.

f.g: ‘Brass’ in the KJV usually means bronze (copper and tin).

n: The “molten sea” was a giant cast-bronze basin, about 15 feet across and 7½ feet deep. Its size declared the greatness of God and the importance of being clean before Him.

f.g: A great cast-metal water basin; ‘sea’ suggests its vastness.

n: Rows of ox figures were cast into the bowl beneath its rim, made in one piece with it. (1 Kings 7:24 describes these as gourds, perhaps a related decorative pattern.)

f.g: Likeness or image.

n: The sea rested on twelve bronze oxen, three facing each direction. The twelve likely represented the tribes of Israel; Latter-day Saint temple baptismal fonts follow this same pattern.

f.g: Rear ends; the oxen faced outward with their backs toward the center.

n: The bronze was a hand’s width thick, and its rim curved outward like a cup or lily blossom. It held about 3,000 baths — perhaps 17,000 gallons. (1 Kings gives 2,000 baths, perhaps a different measuring method.)

f.g: About 3 inches (7.5 cm).

n: Ten smaller basins on wheeled stands were placed on either side for rinsing the sacrificial parts, while the great sea was for the priests’ own washing. Purity was required both of the offering and the one offering.

f.g: Washing basins.

n: Ten golden lampstands, made to the prescribed pattern, lined the holy place — five on each side — filling the house with light.

f.g: According to the pattern ordained for them.

n: Ten tables (for the bread of the Presence) were placed in the holy place, and a hundred golden bowls were made, likely for sprinkling sacrificial blood.

f.g: Bowls used for sprinkling or pouring.

n: Solomon built an inner court for the priests and a larger outer court for the people, with bronze-covered doors between them.

f.g: The inner court, also called the ‘inner court’ in Kings.

n: The great sea was set at the southeast corner of the temple building.

f.g: Toward the south side.

n: Huram the craftsman finished the remaining bronze work — pots for removing ashes, shovels, and bowls — completing his assignment for Solomon.
A summary list of Huram’s work: the two pillars with their bowl-shaped capitals and the decorative lattice wreaths covering them.

f.g: Bowl-shaped or rounded parts of the column capitals.
Lattice or network ornaments.

n: Four hundred pomegranates hung in two rows around each lattice wreath of the pillar capitals.
Huram also made the wheeled stands and the basins that sat upon them.

f.g: Movable bronze stands on wheels.

n: He made the one great sea and the twelve oxen beneath it.
All the bronze utensils were made of polished bronze by Huram, here honored as “his father” — likely a title of respect meaning master craftsman.

f.g: See 2 Chronicles 2:13; ‘father’ here is probably an honorific.
Polished or burnished bronze.

n: The large bronze pieces were cast in clay molds in the Jordan valley, where the clay soil was ideal for casting.

f.g: A town east of the Jordan river.
Called Zarethan in 1 Kings 7:46; location near the Jordan.

n: So much bronze was used that no one even tried to weigh it. The abundance reflects both Solomon’s wealth and David’s preparation.

f.g: Could not be determined or calculated.

n: Solomon also made the gold furnishings for the interior: the golden incense altar and the tables for the bread of the Presence.
The pure-gold lampstands were to burn before the inner sanctuary as the law required.

f.g: According to the prescribed ordinance.
The inner sanctuary — the most holy place.

n: Even the decorative flowers, lamps, and tongs were made of the finest gold.

f.g: The purest, completely refined gold.

n: Wick trimmers, bowls, spoons, and incense pans were pure gold, and the doors to the holy place and most holy place were gold too. Approaching God’s presence meant moving inward toward ever greater holiness.

f.g: Tools to trim lamp wicks.
Pans for carrying burning coals and incense.
